utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. A few procedural matters. First of all, the Chamber will still have to decide on the 92 ter motion in relation to Witness JF-034 which is the witness who will testify today. Mr. Weber, no protective measures; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bogunovic, we'll do that in the usual way. If there is anything the parties would want to add in addition to what their response was on the July 2007, we'd like to hear, otherwise we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same for you, Mr. Bakrac. Then the second issue very briefly. On the 10th of June, the Stanisic Defence has submitted a request for certain questions to be put to Dr. Eekhof. On the 24th of June, the Prosecution has filed its response and apparently have no objections against these questions to be put to Dr. Eekhof. The Chamber grants the request and invites Dr. Eekhof to file his answers to these questions in a week, and the Registrar is requested, first of all, to relay the questions put by the Stanisic Defence to Dr. Eekhof, and also inform him that the Chamber would very much like to receive responses to those questions within a week from now. Next brief matter, the Chamber would invite the parties to make submissions, at least if they wish to do so, with regard to increased number of sittings days per week after the recess, which would result in speeding up the pace of this trial. The Chamber is a aware of the recently filed motion for a non-sitting week after the recess. We'll consider that, but, Mr. Bakrac, your request for additional time which is focusing on Mr. Simatovic, of course, is a matter not exactly the same as speeding up, that is, sitting more days a week after the recess. So if you'd like -- if you wish to make submissions on that, you are invited to do so, and the same is true for the Stanisic Defence. We'd like to receive any submissions on this matter before the -- not later than the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to make submissions, but we would like the submissions to be based on the most up-to-date view by Dr. Eekhof as to what would be reasonable. I don't know if Your Honours would wish then that we construct some questions to put to Eekhof in a way we have done for provisional release or if Your Honours would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll, consider -- I -- of course the Chamber is aware of all of the reports that have been filed and now and then there are problems and sometimes it was relatively unproblematic. But, if there are any specific questions you would like to raise with Dr. Eekhof, I think it would be the best way that you would submit him to the Chamber first and we deal with that in a similar way as with the questions in relation to travelling -- capability of travelling and these kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as then we could receive input from Dr. Eekhof as well. Then finally, the Chamber has admitted P380, P382, P385, P387, on the 22nd of July. Earlier we had suggested that the Prosecution would file a chart indicating for each document which parts of the documents are particularly relevant and further explaining the probative value. The decision on admission stands, but the Prosecution is nevertheless requested to file such a chart in order to assist the Chamber in attaching the appropriate weight to the documents. Now, the Chamber can imagine, Mr. Groome, that you would leave one column in that chart open and that you give an opportunity to the Defence to fill that column with Defence comments and wait with filing your chart for one week to see whether there's any additional Defence comments in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then for the Defence, would you carefully look at the chart that Mr. Groome will propose and if you do not add your comments within a week from disclosure of the draft chart by the Prosecution, then the Chamber will understand it as if you have no comments. I mean, the documents are admitted into evidence, that has been done already. Finally, I'd like to put on the record that where earlier the OTP had informed the Chamber that the Mladic diaries were all disclosed in translation, that that was a mistake, I do understand that we -- we have granted four weeks for the Defence to respond to. Now, of course those four weeks will start once disclosure is complete in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand. I apologise. It was the original scans that were available last week. I believe a fair number of them have been disclosed in English, but that process will be completed next week sometime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber would like to be kept updated on where we stand because otherwise it's a bit difficult for us to keep an eye on the four-weeks time-limit we've set. If there's no other matter, I have no further issues to raise. I would then invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, as I do understand it's Mr. Bogunovic who will testify through videolink from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Adam Weber on behalf of the Prosecution. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll see whether the videolink functions adequately. Could I hear from the representative of the Registry in Belgrade whether she can hear us and whether she can see us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can hear you and see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely because it was not plugged in the right socket, could you please repeat what you just said. I saw you speaking, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can hear you and we can see you. Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can hear you, we can see you. If you speak one or two more words then we'll verify but at least all the Judges are able to hear you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we all can hear you. And could you please tell us who is with you in the room where you are in at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] In this moment is just one representative of the Registry and one technician. The witness is awaiting in the witness room and we can bring him in right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please bring the witness in to the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a loud-speaker so the witness doesn't have to wear any headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Witness is in the video-link room, Your Honour, now and he has his headphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. Can you hear me, can you see me, Mr. Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now in front of you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration. Please stand for it. Could you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogunovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogunovic. Can you see me on your monitor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see you. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I couldn't hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borislav Bogunovic. I was born on the 25th of March, 1950 in Negoslavci, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you provide two statements to investigators from the ICTY on the 6th of June, 2003, and the 8th of February, 2007?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity prior to testifying here today to review your prior statements in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions that you were asked during these previous statements, would you provide the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders 65 ter 5301, which is the 2003 ICTY statement; and 65 ter 5302, the 2007 ICTY statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, it's not uncommon that we identify the relevant statements with the witness. Now, there's hardly any chance that there's any fake statement. If there's any doubt as to that, I would like to hear from the Defence, otherwise, we could proceed. There appears to be no reason not to proceed. Mr. Registrar, would you please assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 5301 will be P553. And 65 ter 5302 will be P554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections to admission? No objections. P553 and P554 are admitted into evidence. Yes, Mr. Weber, nevertheless, you go over the formalities very quickly. Perhaps I put one or two questions to the witness in this respect. Mr. Bogunovic, when you gave these statements at the time, did you answer the question in accordance with the truth to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, when you reviewed those statements, did you recognise them as the statements you gave at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 60 of Exhibit P553, you confirm a route driven between Backa Palanka to Vukovar via Sarengrad in a video. Did you again have occasion to see this video on the 24th of June, 2010, and did you confirm that this route is depicted at minute marker 503 to 624 of the video?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders the two associated exhibits to Exhibit P553. The first associated exhibit is a photo array under Prosecution 65 ter 4640. The second associated exhibit is a video under 65 ter 2839. The Prosecution is only tendering the first 9 minutes and 1 second of 65 ter 2839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that what you uploaded is limited to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections? No objections. Mr. Registrar, the photo array 4640 and the video 2839 will receive what numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 65 ter 4640 will receive Exhibit P555, Your Honour. And the 65 ter 2839 will receive Exhibit P556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P555 and P556 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Chamber's instructions of 18 February 2010, the Prosecution requests leave at this time to present a public witness summary of the evidence of Borislav Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you explained to the witness the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I did during proofing, but I don't know if the Chamber would like to remind him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, Mr. Weber will now read a summary of your statement that is to inform the public what your testimony is about. However, the evidence is in your statements themselves. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Borislav Bogunovic is the former minister of the interior of the SAO SBWS government. Prior to becoming the minister of interior, Mr. Bogunovic was elected vice-president of the SDS party in Vukovar in May of 1990. On 7 January 1991, the Serb National Council of the SBWS was established and the witness was appointed vice-president of the council by Goran Hadzic. In August 1991, the SAO SBWS government was formed in Dalj. In his capacity of minister of interior, the witness was part of the establishment of the Serb police force of the SAO SBWS. Although Mr. Bogunovic was appointed minister of interior, the decisions regarding the SBWS police force were made in Belgrade. Mr. Bogunovic personally met with Jovica Stanisic on three to four occasions throughout the fall of 1991. The witness provides evidence that whenever Jovica Stanisic had to talk to anyone from the SAO SBWS government, he would do it with Goran Hadzic and with Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza. The witness states that Badza received operational orders directly from Belgrade and he would then discuss these orders with Goran Hadzic. The SBWS police force was equipped with uniforms and guns by the Serbian MUP in Novi Sad and Badza acted as a co-ordinator with the Serbian MUP by providing Mr. Bogunovic with guide-lines on what to do. After the establishment of the police forces in Borovo Selo and Dalj, other police stations were opened. The equipment, included luxury cars, were supplied by the Novi Sad SUP. The salaries for the SBWS police came from Novi Sad as the SBWS had no monetary system and could not exist without the full support of Serbia. The evidence of this witness is that Hadzic was controlled by the authorities in Belgrade and that Arkan was not under the control of the JNA as he was under the control of the Serbian MUP and Jovica Stanisic. At the end of August 1991, Mr. Bogunovic relocated his office from Dalj to Sid and later when Vukovar was taken over by the Serbian forces, Mr. Bogunovic set up the office in Ilok at the end of November 1991. The Red Berets appeared in Ilok at the beginning of December 1991 and the witness learned that Franko Simatovic, aka Frenki, was the person who gave them orders. Mr. Bogunovic states that the Red Berets created some problems in Ilok as they were carry out arbitrary checks and searches on vehicles and their occupants. The Red Berets often confiscated vehicles that were never returned to the lawful owners. For this reason, Mr. Bogunovic requested the army to intervene. After a December 1991 meeting with Jovica Stanisic and Badza, Mr. Bogunovic was subsequently removed as minister of the interior of the SAO SBWS. At this time the Prosecution would note for the Chamber's reference that the locations discussed by this witness can be found on map 18 admitted as Exhibit P9 and map 37 admitted as part of P258. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, in paragraph 18 of Exhibit P554, it is your evidence that Slobodan Milosevic controlled Goran Hadzic through Arkan and Badza, and Stanisic was the link between Milosevic and Arkan and Badza. Your testimony today will focus on your experiences with these individuals and the matter in which this impression became known to you. Did you know that these connections existed when the SDS party was formed in Vukovar in May of 1990?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time. I didn't know what the links were, but I was aware that we were definitely, you know, in some way connected with Ivan Raskovic as it turned out later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Jovan Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was our belief that Jovan Raskovic and his associates went regularly to Belgrade and that that was the link with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Between the formation of the SDS party in May of 1990 and the establishment of the Serb National Council on 7th January, 1991, did you become aware of any communications between Goran Hadzic and Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic mentioned going to Belgrade, and he said that there he would meet Slobodan Milosevic. He would then convey that to us during various meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of Exhibit P554, you state that Goran Hadzic went to Belgrade a number of times during 1991 to meet with Stanisic and with Slobodan Milosevic. I know that because in government meetings Hadzic often mentioned these meetings. When did you become aware of Hadzic going to these meetings in Belgrade in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I became aware of it during a meeting when Goran told all of us that he had been to Belgrade and that he had an agreement with President Milosevic to go on with our work and establish a government. He also said that we enjoyed their support and that everyone was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How often would Goran Hadzic go to Belgrade to meet with Slobodan Milosevic between January 1991 and the formation of the SAO SBWS government in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was on several occasions. On several occasions he conveyed a messages to us. I'm not sure that he informed us about all of his visits, but those visits probably happened five or six times during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you first hear of Jovica Stanisic being present at these meetings in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Goran told us that. He told us that he went to visit President Milosevic together with Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately when did Goran Hadzic tell you about this meeting with Jovica Stanisic and President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: He told us that on the eve of the setting up of the SAO Krajina government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you hear of Jovica Stanisic being present at all between meetings from January 1991 to August 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could learn from Hadzic who informed us about what was going on, I would say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When is the earliest point in time that you heard of Jovica Stanisic being present at meetings in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that sometime after the 1st of May, after the conflicts broke out in Borovo Selo. That was when he informed us that Jovica Stanisic had also attended a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Between May and August 1991, how often did Hadzic go to Belgrade for these meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think, or rather, as far as I know from his reports during that period he attended such meetings about four times, meetings in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You state in the same paragraph, this is paragraph 15 of Exhibit P554, that Hadzic would come back from Belgrade with instructions on what to do. What instructions were provided to Hadzic between May and August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: These instructions were as follows: We were supposed to set up a government, we were supposed to have our representatives who would represent the people of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. All that boiled down to our task to set up a government. We were supposed to see what we would do with the produce that was produced in the area, and we were also supposed to provide security for the corridor that would allow people to get supplies, to get to the doctors, and that was supposed to be done by the military. The military were supposed to provide security for those who wanted to pass through that corridor, and we were also supposed to try to enable the people of the area to work and live and move about without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What members of the Serb National Council were told of these meetings by Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Koncarevic, Ilija Petrovic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Miodrag Crnogorac, Boro Milinkovic, and perhaps some others who I don't remember at the moment, but I would say that those were the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whose instructions did you believe were being implemented by the Serb National Council of the SBWS prior to August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we had a lot of things that were imposed upon us by the situation. However, I was also convinced that Goran was receiving instructions from Belgrade and whenever he came back from there, he brought new instructions for us as to how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After the government of the SAO SBWS was formed in August of 1991, how often did Goran Hadzic go to Belgrade and receive instructions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: When Hadzic became the president of the government, he went to Belgrade but more often he went to Novi Sad. We didn't have our monetary system, we didn't have our tender, so we had to deal with the problem of salaries for the police and everybody else. And at that time we were closer to Novi Sad, and as I say, Goran Hadzic did get to Belgrade, but more often he went to Novi Sad where he dealt with the matters that faced both him and all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where in Novi Sad would Goran Hadzic go for meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic attended those meetings at the regional government or the regional council, and that's where he discussed problems that prevailed at the time, mainly the sale of the agricultural produce and its transportation to Serbia. We could not sell our produce anywhere else. That was one thing. And there was also another thing and that was to implement some ideas and deal with some problems that we faced. The first problem was funding that we didn't have or finances, in general. And the second thing was helping us with the work of the government. With our work we did not have much experience. We had just started doing our jobs, executing our tasks and we needed help with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Between August and December 1991, what instructions were provided during -- provided to Hadzic during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: According to those instructions, we were supposed to help our residents to see how they could get by some money. All the goods were in short supply and the supplies were getting shorter by the day. So there was a problem with supplies, with the money, things had to be brought over from Serbia and vice-versa. Things had to be transported to Serbia. Also, there was a need for us to inform both people in Belgrade as well as people in Novi Sad about what was going on in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Goran Hadzic receive any instructions on what ministers to appoint to the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, objection. Unless my learned friend is referring to a part of the statement, he must be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a particular point in the statement. I believe the witness has generally discussed they received instructions on how to set up the government of the SAO SBWS. I can phrase it a little bit more broadly by saying what, if any. There are many instructions that were provided many times, I'm just trying to get directly to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please rephrase it and because it seems that instructions appear clearly in the statement but not necessarily what type of instructions and what these instructions covered as we find it in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I also make the point that I again cannot find anything about the regional government in Novi Sad giving instructions to Hadzic in the statements. This is a whole -- I might be wrong, but this looks as though it's a whole new subject which my learned friend has discussed with the witness but not disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The witness's meanings and providing -- I don't want to say too much in front of the witness in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put questions to the witness, could you refer, as much as you can, to the part of the statement you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will. The witness has discussed at length what was going on in Novi Sad and what was provided from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you perhaps in order to inform Mr. Jordash and the Chamber about what parts of the statement you are referring to with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, what, if any, instructions were provided to Hadzic concerning the appointment of ministers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the party provided proposals for the appointment of ministers and that was normal. However, there were also people whom we didn't know at the time. They did not reside in the SBWS territory. They were Caslav Ocic from Belgrade. Ilija Koncarevic from Novi Sad, Ilija Petrovic from Novi Sad, and I don't know if there was anybody else. We provided our proposals and Goran told us that those men that I have just mentioned should also be appointed as ministers. Most of us, or rather, none of us knew them. We had seen Koncarevic and Petrovic at some prior meetings. I don't know how they happened to find themselves among us, but I can say that people who resided in the territory of that area I knew them but as for the others, we did not propose them, we did not know anything about them until the moment Goran informed us that they would be put forth for those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Goran inform you of the reason he was putting forth certain individuals for appointment as ministers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The reason that he mentioned was the fact that those people were necessary to establish the necessary links between us and Belgrade and Novi Sad. That's what he had been told and that's the message that he conveyed to us. He recommended that we should accept that proposal and we did finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have Exhibit P16 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, there was some misunderstanding. May I take it that you want to have P16 which is in evidence on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was some confusion with the Registrar. That's how I understood you, but -- so what you wanted to say is, could I please have Exhibit P16, which is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, can you see the document that is now before you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the "Official Gazette" publication listing the ministers of the government of the SAO SBWS. Who on this list did Hadzic receive instructions to appointment? If you could please just go down it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have to object to this line of questions. This does not in any form appear in the disclosure. This is a matter which my learned friend has discussed with the witness at length, has obviously got notes and has chosen not to disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it what Mr. Weber has done apparently is not for you to tell us, but you say it's not part of the disclosure, whatever he may have discussed or not discussed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is part of the disclosure is Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see what Mr. Weber's answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's two statements. There's two proofing notes -- three proofing notes, and another third statement that has been taken from this witness. I'm showing him an item in evidence and in conjunction with a rather short proofing note last week, there was information concerning information about an appointment of the minister. This witness throughout his evidence has testified that there were instructions received by Goran Hadzic on how to set up the government of the SAO SBWS. This falls well in the confines of that notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The proofing note, of course, first of all, is not in evidence, but second is, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult for the Chamber to decide because we have not seen any proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can inform the Court that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I just want to caution is because the witness hasn't given an answer if Mr. Jordash could refrain from providing any substantive information in whatever his comments are going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can put it this way: That the disclosure that we have received does not -- concerning the appointment of one minister, does not include the last 20 minutes of evidence and the ministers mentioned therein. And, Your Honour, I did put my objection in the way that I did, that my learned friend has discussed this with the witness, because it's clearly the witness and counsel knows where they are going with this. The only people who don't know are us in the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has testified that Goran Hadzic received instructions on how to set up the government of SAO SBWS. I'm just showing him an exhibit and asking him who, and that's all I'm doing. This is within the confines of his noticed evidence for this witness and who he was and his relationships with these other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, my learned friend is right. We did receive notice that this witness was going to say Hadzic received instructions from Milosevic. And then we received a proofing note in June detailing that one particular person was appointed as a minister because of the first accused, and that is it in relation to what, in fact, Hadzic received instructions to do. So, yes, we have received an extremely generalised disclosure on the issue and my learned friend's submission amounts to, well, we can fill in the details as we go along in Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of the 2003 statement going back there is a sentence in there, there were also discussions in Novi Sad and Belgrade about the formation of the government. He details how early that occurred. He names many of the other people throughout his statement that were included in those discussions, talks in paragraph 7 about prior to the formation of that government. Mentions an individual that he has just mentioned today. If counsel could please actually read through the statements before making accusations towards the Prosecution in this regard. We are just following through on what this witness's disclosed evidence has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to cut this short. Apparently instructions and setting up of the government is a, as I understand you well, is a rather general issue and to go into all kind of details which could have elicited during these interviews would have put you on notice of what actually Mr. Weber is asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In fact, it's worse than that, Your Honour. They -- the paragraph of the statement my learned friend has just discussed do summarise the position, and the position is summarised at paragraph 6 where the witness speaks of discussions with Milosevic, discussions and meetings between Hadzic and persons in Belgrade, and approvals of certain decisions made by those local to the SBWS. So we have at one point in time disclosure saying the decisions were made locally and approved in Belgrade, and now what we have is a complete reversal, that decisions were being made in Belgrade and sent to SBWS, and then on top of that non-disclosure of what those decisions were, in fact, the decisions I mean emanating from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection, although it also expresses that, Mr. Weber, it's not as clear-cut as you say it. It would have been preferable to have more of the details you are apparently interested in now in the statement so that it would have been disclosed to the Defence. We'll see how it develops and we'll also see whether this would trigger any further need for preparations from the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, on the document that appears before you, could you please tell us who on this list did Hadzic receive instructions to appoint?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see here at that meeting we did not discuss the matter of Ilija Kojic being the defence minister. Caslav Ocic was not supposed to be a minister for foreign affairs. This came as a surprise. However, we finally ended up accepting Goran Hadzic's explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You just mentioned Ilija Kojic. How was Ilija Kojic appointed to being defence minister?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed upon Mr. Goran Hadzic's proposal once he was appointed president of the government. As I said, the party had not put his name forth. It was at Goran Hadzic's proposal that we appointed him. Goran Hadzic had the right to put forth proposals, and he proposed Ilija Kojic and Caslav Ocic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell Goran Hadzic to appoint Ilija Kojic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, as I've just said, that came as a surprise to us. However, he said that such a move was necessary, that he himself believed that that should be done, and we went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have shown to the witness page 2 of the B/C/S and English versions of Exhibit P407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could I ask one or two additional questions to the witness. Mr. Bogunovic, do I understand you well that in your discussions you came up with proposals and suggestions of people to be appointed and that finally most of them were approved but not all of them, is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid I did not hear you well. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand you well that you during your conversations you suggested and you proposed names of those to be appointed and that then your suggestions or proposals would be approved by Belgrade, but that this did not always happen, that sometimes others were appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, there were such instances as well. We put forth our proposals. We conveyed those proposals to Goran Hadzic, and it happened often times that he had to see, he had to think about it, and then finally he would come up with his own proposals, and he explained that the people he proposed were well connected in Belgrade or lived there and so on and so forth. In any case, he urged us to approve his proposals and to act upon them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression that the visits of Mr. Hadzic to Belgrade were of any influence to the final appointments specifically in relation to those persons you had not proposed or suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you explained that he told you what the good reasons were to appoint other persons than the ones you suggested, you gained the impression that this was discussed and/or supported by those to whom Mr. Hadzic talked in Belgrade; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As soon as our proposal was not accepted, that meant that there must have been another counter-proposal that Goran would go along with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what role would Belgrade have played in those other proposals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the way I saw it at the time, it seems that people who were appointed were those who would certainly keep them posted at all times about what we were doing in the government and what was happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say keep them posted, who are you referring it to when you say "them?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably someone from the government or Milosevic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean Belgrade government circles; is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please show to the witness P407. At this time the Prosecution requests that the report not be broadcast to the public. Page 2 of both the B/C/S and English versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, in the first paragraph of this Serbian state security report, it describes a conflict between Ilija Kojic and Miroljub Vujovic. Do you know what this conflict is about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Counsel, if you like, it's on paragraph 22 of the 2008 proofing note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you right away that the rift between the two was actually with Vujovic on one side who was a representative of the Territorial Defence and he was at the helm of it and Ilija Kojic on the other, who was at the head of the Ministry of Defence at the time. There was an argument between the two and at some point things got a bit too far. Basically they almost engaged in open clashes. The person who tried to calm the tension was Mr. Visic who was the municipal president. He tried to act as a go-between to reduce tensions and to prevent any potential bloodshed and victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was the reason that Kojic wanted Vujovic to topple the chief of the Vukovar SUP?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for that was because Vujovic followed a certain line, and he had people who had fought with him in battle-fields. An argument ensued between him and Kojic because he believed that he was not supposed to hold that position and that he wasn't doing things the way people expected him to, or at least those fighters believed things should be run.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The second paragraph of this report indicates that the assistant minister of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, tried to use Slobodan Ivkovic, Ilija Kojic, and Kostic, and others to turn the Krajina into a "twilight zone." Was there any connection or are you aware of any connection between Jovica Stanisic and Ilija Kojic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe there must have been a connection between the two because Ilija Kojic at the time was the defence minister. They probably had some points in common, although I cannot be any more specific than that. In any case, I believe they must have been in touch and that they had their own arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What did you either directly see or hear that led you to believe this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We had meetings about those events. Hadzic was in a way circumvented as the president as well as we in the government. This was at the apex of the rift between the minister of defence and the Territorial Defence. At that time the minister of defence of Krajina was included as well. And one could clearly see that the police and the military had gone their own separate ways. They could not reach an agreement about some things that were taking place at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of licence plates did Ilija Kojic have on his car?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The registration plates on Ilija Kojic's car were that of the MUP of Serbia with an M.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did any other ministers have licence plates with the same registration?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 56 of Exhibit P553, you state that there were Territorial Defence staffs in the territories that were freed and they were responsible to the minister of defence, Ilija Kojic. He was the one who co-ordinated the Territorial Defence with the JNA. My question to you is, who controlled the Territorial Defence of the SAO SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1991 the TO was controlled by the army. They had to co-ordinate their activities with the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "they had to co-ordinate," who was the "they" that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The TO, or rather, TO staffs and army staffs. They had to be in co-ordination and co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is a time for a break or not, but this would be a good breaking point for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber. And how much time would you still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Still have a ways to go. A full session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Full session. But the initial assessment was two hours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, and this is the first session so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two sessions is not the same as two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate. So I believe I will use whatever the two hour allotted time is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you are ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 45 of Exhibit P553, you indicate that: "Although Arkan was not a member of government, he would occasionally attend meetings. It was my impression that he did that in order to control some ministers." What gave you the impression that Arkan attended meetings in order to control some of the ministers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It depended very much on the agenda of a meeting. Occasionally Arkan would come in, sit down, and listen to what we were discussing so as to be familiar with what was being discussed at such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would there be times that Arkan took a more active role in the meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: He wouldn't say much, only on occasion. Mostly after a government session would finish, he would leave with Hadzic and then the two of them probably discussed what was discussed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the relationship between Goran Hadzic and Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that Arkan's seat was in Erdut, much as Goran's. They met in the morning usually, and they were constantly in touch, unless Arkan was somewhere in the field outside of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 23 of Exhibit P554, you state that you got the impression that Arkan and Badza operated on the same level with no subordination between each other. They were both trusted by the Belgrade establishment so they had freedom in the field. What gave you the impression that Arkan and Badza operated on the same level with no subordination between them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I got that impression because they met daily and co-operated. I know that Arkan had his men, whom he took into action. He did things of his own accord, at least much of what he did was done in that way. I can't say whether the two of them discussed things they were going to do frequently. I only know that they were together frequently. And that's what gave me the impression that they worked on things jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you or other members of the SAO SBWS government would discuss matters with Arkan and Badza, did Arkan and Badza indicate who they had to contact?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they never did so. They never said who had sent them and who they were in contact with. They didn't share that with us. Goran was aware of it and perhaps some other people, but I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P54 marked for identification for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, this is a certificate issued by the supreme headquarters of the Territorial Defence of the SAO SBWS dated 13 December 1991. The certificate states it is issued in order to regulate the employment status of the named individual and is signed by commander Radovan Stojicic. Why would certificates regulating the employment of TO members have been issued by Badza?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the certificate speaks for itself. It was used to justify leave absence. As you can see here, Badza appears here as the commander. It surprised me a bit when I saw this document because he never referred to himself as the commander, but we can see him signing this, and this explains what his role was in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp on this document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise it as the stamp of the Territorial Defence of Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders Exhibit P54 into evidence. It was originally marked for identification on the 27th of August, 2009, with Witness B-215 pending the witness's return for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. P54 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 of Exhibit P554 you state: "Regarding the financing of the SAO SBWS police force, I have to state that the money came from Novi Sad. On the other hand, there was no monetary system in the SAO SBWS. We had no funds." This paragraph concludes: "I could say that the SAO SBWS was a virtual government. It existed on paper but, in fact, we could not do anything without Serbia's support." What do you mean when you state that the SAO SBWS government could not do anything without Serbia's support?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was clear to everyone that without the support and co-operation from Serbia we would not have been able to do anything. We did not have our monetary system, our own finances that we could use to pay the police at first and later on the other bodies. That was the first precondition. We had to provide our agricultural produce, that was for the most part taken to Novi Sad and Vojvodina. And in return, we received money. That is how we managed to keep the government and police going. That's how we paid people working for the government and the public servants we employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 2635, page 2 in the English and page 1 in the B/C/S, placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the budget of the government of the SAO SBWS for the year 1991 as published in the "Official Gazette." Under Article 1 of the budget, it states that the total revenue of the SAO SBWS for the year 1991 amounts to just over 27 million dinars. Did the government of the SAO SBWS have over 27 million dinars available as revenue?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that by May 2, 1992 the situation in the area was normal. There was no existing problems in terms of payment. We followed the system that had been used in the Republic of Croatia. Only after our government had been formed we established our Ministry of Finance. However, what you see here is something we didn't really have. This was only the final amount for that current year in terms of revenue and expenditure, but I don't know how anyone arrived at these figures. As I said, much of it -- much of the system did not operate. In my opinion, this is fictitious so as to put something on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under Article 5 of the budget, the sources of revenues are individually listed. Could you please review these sources and tell us if the government of the SAO SBWS collected revenues from these sources in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the English version this carries over to page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me start with first things first. The surplus of revenues --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- I don't know where that started from. There are many --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Unfortunately I'm limited on time. I was wondering if you could just please look at these listed sources of revenue and let us know simply whether or not the SAO SBWS actually collected revenue from these sources?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it then a correct understanding that the SAO SBWS did not collect revenue from these sources?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you would be right there. It didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This exhibit reflects that Ilija Koncarevic issued this decision. Why would Ilija Koncarevic be the individual to issue a decision on the budget?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Koncarevic was the president of the Assembly at the time. I don't know. It's very hard for me to understand that that was not done by the minister of finance or the president of the government. I really don't know how come that it was Ilija Koncarevic who did that and not somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders 12 exhibits into evidence. We are requesting separate exhibit numbers for each of the exhibits. These Exhibits are laws, decisions, and minutes of the government of the SAO SBWS. A chart individually listing these exhibits was provided before the proceedings today. Prosecution 65 ter 2635 is included on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we find in the chart specific portions which we have to pay attention to the specific areas of relevance in those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They are the laws that were in effect. I believe there's a description of each of the exhibits as to what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it sounds very much like bar table tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that we have certain rules for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a witness on the stand that could authenticate each and every one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not about authentication. It's about large amount of texts coming in where the Chamber of course has got no idea yet on whether the number 10 conclusions of the Assembly whether everything is relevant or certain portions are relevant. And I think the system is that you make a chart, that you point at the specific areas of relevance which the Chamber could focus on when reading it, then that there would be a column for the Defence in which they could give their comments as to whether they challenge the relevance of that or whether they want to draw our attention to other elements of those documents so that the Chamber can work in a more focused way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Be happy to do whatever the Chamber would like. We have discussed it with both Defence and there's no opposition to the admission of these. I believe the parties have spoken about it and in accordance with the nature of these discussions, believe it is most efficient at this time to seek admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just, if -- I see 12 minutes from the 18th session of the SAO SBWS held on the 28th of November in Erdut. Not all of it is direct relevance to the case. It may be that that's different here, but then the Chamber wants to know what paragraph, what pages require our specific attention for this case. I think that, Mr. Groome, also looking at you, I think we've explained this at earlier occasions. To make a chart and identify the specific relevant portions of documents or if the document is a short document, to describe in half a line what the relevance is, then give an opportunity to the Defence to add that and then make a bar table submission of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, we may, can reserve exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have at least 65 ter 2635 admitted at this time. The witness has provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest -- I suggest, we have here 12 bar table documents that we'll reserve 12 numbers for them, and that once we've received the submission in which we can read what the relevance is and where the Defence has been given an opportunity to either draw attention to other relevant portions or to challenge the relevance and say this is a mistake that, that we then finally decide on admission. Mr. Registrar, the numbers would be, the numbers to be reserved are?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number that will be reserved for the 12 65 ter numbers are P557 up to P568, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And already, Mr. Weber, in this system P561 would correspond with 65 ter 2635. Any objection because that's not bar tabled, that's introduced through the witness? Then P561 is admitted into evidence and the other numbers we are waiting for your chart explaining relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your previous statements you describe personally meeting with Jovica Stanisic on three to four occasions. In paragraph 14 of Exhibit P554, you discuss a late August 1991 meeting in Novi Sad in the Vojvodina building -- excuse me, the Vojvodina police building. What is the reason that you and Hadzic went to this meeting in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The reason we went to Novi Sad was the setting up of police stations in Dalj and Borovo Selo. We went to that to discuss the uniforms for the police and weapons, as well as communications means and a couple of vehicles that would be used by our police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 of Exhibit P553 you state that: "Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza, was with the Serbian MUP, acted as co-ordinator and gave us guide-lines on what to do. He was the one who said we could go to Novi Sad and get the uniforms and equipment." How did Badza co-ordinate this meeting in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Badza co-ordinated the meeting through Goran Hadzic. He told him that we should go to Novi Sad and that I should go as the minister of the interior and we were supposed to discuss the hand-over of all the aforementioned things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this meeting the first time that you met Jovica Stanisic in person?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that was the first or the second time. I believe that it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did this meeting in Novi Sad last?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was rather short. A decision was reached to give us what we had requested. Near Novi Sad there is a place called Klisa. That's where the police depo was. Some 10 or 15 meetings after the meeting I went there to that place called Klisa and from there we obtained the uniforms and all the other things that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who did this police depot belong to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: To the MUP of Vojvodina, or rather, to the regional secretariat in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And the MUP of Vojvodina is a part of what MUP?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the uniforms that were provided to you for the police forces of the SAO SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The uniforms were the same as the uniforms of the Serbian police. Trousers, jackets, short-barrelled weapons, just like the police in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What colour were these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say short-barrelled weapons, what type of weapons were provided to you from this depot in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the red Zastava pistols calibre 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where were these pistols licensed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they were licensed. We took them over. I signed the receipt, and I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of Exhibit P554, you discuss a meeting with Jovica Stanisic in Backa Palanka that took place in the autumn of 1991. Do you recall the month in which this meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can remember the meeting took place in late October or early November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You indicate that Jovica Stanisic, Hadzic, Ljubo Novakovic, and some other people from Novi Sad whom you did not know were present. How did you know the other people that were there were from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that from conversations. They discussed the assistance to the displaced persons and people in Slavonia. They were to be accommodated in Ilok and while they were in the Sports Hall there, reference was made to Novi Sad from where the toiletries should have been obtained, as well as groceries. Backa Palanka is a small municipality and could not provide all that, so they said that we should go to Novi Sad if we wanted to obtain all those supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the office of the Backa Palanka municipality president.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting lasted for an hour and a half, or at least that's how long I was there and that's how long the discussions took before any conclusions were reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After this meeting, did you relocate your offices to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: After that meeting we had another meeting of the government in Erdut, and I was told to move my offices to Ilok together with another minister, Vojo Susa. A couple of days later, we set up our stuff, or rather, our office where we continued to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who told you to move your office to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Ilok, were there any problems?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When Croats left Ilok, about five to six Croats left, and the equal number of people were settled there from other municipalities in Croatia, some 4 to 5.000 of them. And they were all to be accommodated in houses or apartments. They were all to be provided with food and the bare necessities to sustain them during the first few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of Exhibit P554 you state that there were some conflicts between our police force and the Red Berets and there were complaints from civilians. Allegedly the Red Berets took some vehicles from local populations and for their own use. The Red Berets would go into houses of civilians, all of them Serbs, Slovaks, Croats to request vehicles for the use of the TO. But the vehicles were never returned to their legitimate owners. When did the Red Berets arrive in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date. However, towards the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992, the first Red Berets appeared. I didn't know who had sent them or why, but they were there. They arrived in a somewhat bigger house. They were billeted there, and that's where their headquarters was. On a couple of occasions, there were problems involving the Red Berets and the people working at the police and the citizens of Ilok. There were cases when they took vehicles and that was allowed at the time, but they were supposed to provide a receipt. The vehicles should have been confiscated for a limited duration of time. However, when they took the vehicles that they did, they did not provide any receipts and, any documents to that effect. The vehicles were simply taken from their owners and never returned to them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you learn who the commander of the Red Berets in Ilok was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not everything that the witness has said has been interpreted. The witness also said how many such cases there were, and I don't see that that has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean vehicles being taken, how often that happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe this matter can either be explored on cross-examination or the parties can request a verification of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Weber. If there is what seems to be an obvious lack of translation, I'm not saying there is, we would rather verify that right away so that we know what the evidence is and that we are not missing anything due to it not being translated. Mr. Petrovic, is it there were cases when they took vehicles and that was allowed at the time but they were supposed to provide a receipt, is that where you thought the number was missing? Could you point at the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, both in the line that you read out as well as in the last sentence uttered by the witness. I believe that he indicated on two occasions how many such cases there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask him. Mr. Bogunovic, did you refer to numbers of those cases where vehicles were taken, and if so, could you tell us what those numbers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said three or four cases. I don't know whether there were any more than that. I can't tell you, I don't remember. It was a long time ago. But I remember that there were complaints by that many citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness has said reflects the gist of the -- what he said before, although he used different words. Maybe it would be useful to listen to that part of his evidence to know exactly what the witness said the first time around. I'm happy with his answer but for the sake of the accuracy of the testimony, maybe it wouldn't be a bad idea to listen to it and to record it just as it was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we've difficulties in listening to the original, that you do so, and elicit from the witness in more detail what he said about it. But I do understand we are talking about small numbers, Mr. Bogunovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, proceed, Mr. Weber. I leave it to you whether you want to seek further clarification at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prosecution appreciates counsel assisting with the matter too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, who did you learn was the commander of the Red Berets in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, I'm afraid. Whose commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Did you learn who the commander of the Red Berets in Ilok was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to what I heard and according to the statements of those people who wore Red Berets, Frenki Simatovic was their commander. That's what I heard from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of Exhibit P553, you indicate that the Red Berets stationed in Ilok would carry out check-ups and searches on their own accord. What kind of check-ups were carried out by the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Red Berets checked both people and vehicles that were moving about. They also went to some houses to check who resided in them and some other similar things. For example, those people who arrived in Ilok had to report to them. They had to be in the know. They had to know who had arrived and who was moving about Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders 65 ter 3836 from the bar table, if permitted. Is a Captain Dragan Fund on file for an individual. The file indicates that the individual was a member of a unit for special purposes of the MUP Serbia under the command of Zivojin Ivanovic, aka Zika Crnogorac, and was injured on the 18th, 19th of December, 1991, near Ilok. This is corroboration of the testimony of this witness. The Prosecution will also note at this time Exhibit P478, the Serbian DB file for Zika Crnogorac which includes a certificate indicating that he is a member of the reserve police force of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia since June 1991. That certificate was signed by Dragoslav Krsmanovic, so we are tendering from the bar table a KDF file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is one single file of which the, I take it the relevance and the probative value has been set out by Mr. Weber. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understood the witness, or rather, the witness's statement corroborated this document. In addition to what the witness said, he didn't say anything else. He did not provide any other knowledge about the Red Beret and what they did in the area. I don't see how anything from the witness's testimony could corroborate this document. I didn't hear it. I didn't see it in his statement. The witness clearly stated that he does not know anything else about the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The witnesses have provided their knowledge. It's corroboration of the fact that the Red Berets in Ilok in December of 1991 as described by the witness, and just to be clear about who the Red Beret unit that we are talking about, we're introducing an item of evidence, a KDF file, that shows that this is a unit that was involved with the MUP of Serbia. That's the reason for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. I don't have the document before me but the document referred to by the Prosecutor has to do with 1993, I believe, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The document refers to the individual who is applying for pension with the Captain Dragan fund who was injured on the 18th, the night of the 18th, morning of the 19th of December, 1991 as a member of the special purpose unit of the MUP under the command of Zika Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrespective of that, Your Honour, this witness provided no basis for that. We can discuss this as a bar table document, but this cannot be relied on as part of this witness's testimony. Perhaps the Prosecutor will reconsider and then submit it as a bar table document, not other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think you introduced it as a bar table document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that objection then is based on a misunderstanding of what Mr. Weber said. Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to make sure I'm accurate in my response. The difficulty that we have with this document is that it does refer to specific combat activity, and it's that which is troublesome. My learned friend says it's introduced to confirm or corroborate that the Red Berets were in Ilok, but the real evidence within that document relates to some combat activity led by Zika, and it's that which a bar table motion would be required to deal with and to explain exactly what that evidence related to and why that was relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's a rather tangential issue. We've explained to the Chamber the reason that we are offering it, and it's to corroborate and confirm the presence of the Red Berets in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue raised by Mr. Petrovic about 1993 is not valid because it deals with 1991, that it should be bar tabled. There is no need to respond to that because there's what Mr. Weber did, and Mr. Weber has sufficiently explained the relevance and the probative value in order for the Chamber to overrule the objection by the Stanisic Defence. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be Exhibit P569, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P569 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of Exhibit P554 you discuss a third meeting in Belgrade with Jovica Stanisic and the SAO Krajina and Serbian governments. Could you please tell us who was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the government building in Serbia. On behalf of the Serbian government there was Mr. Zelenovic who chaired the meeting. I cannot remember the names of all their ministers in attendance. I can only tell you that on our behalf there was Goran Hadzic as president and we as the ministers. We were all there to attend that scheduled meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of Exhibit P554 you indicate that shortly after the meeting in Belgrade, you were removed as the minister of the interior by Badza. How did Badza inform you of this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: At a meeting of the SBWS government Badza was present and he told Mr. Hadzic, the president, that I should be removed due to poor co-ordination and co-operation with him. The issue was that we disagreed on a number of issues, and he suggested that a different person be appointed. This was not accepted by the other ministers at that session. However, at the next session, Goran offered me the place of deputy prime minister in exchange for my position of the minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. I hardly dare to ask who is first and who will be more or less victimised by being the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hardly dare say, but it's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that you have made clear arrangements so as not to curtail the right to cross-examine by the Simatovic Defence. Mr. Petrovic, if at any point you think that you might be at risk to be left sufficient time, then, of course, you either asked to further discuss the matter with Mr. Jordash or you address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, you'll now be cross-examined first by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin, could I clarify with the Chamber how long we might be given so that I can work to that timetable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I see is that the Prosecution used one hour 45 minutes net time. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think if I was trying to be cautious I would say three hours but I hope to finish in two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then have you made arrangements with Mr. Petrovic, how many hours would he need after that? Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my assessment, as it stands now, is up to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
