utterances.text: The Defence is encouraged to see whether they can finish cross-examination together in three hours, but we'll carefully monitor the way in which you use your time, that is, if you would always be very focused and if you would elicit useful evidence, then we might extend that to four hours as you had more or less requested together. At the same time the Chamber is not much inclined to do that if it finds a lot of questions to be either repetitious or not very relevant, et cetera. So we'll also look at the way in which you use your time. That is not very clear guidance, but it is guidance which may encourage you to use your time as efficiently as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to refer, first of all, to P553, your statement of 2003, paragraph 25. You have the statement in front of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it still.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can read the line to you and ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On my screen I see that the witness is provided with a document. Have you got it in front of you now, Mr. Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please go to paragraph 25. The B/C/S paragraphs correspond to the English paragraphs so, yes, paragraph 25 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bogunovic, could you please look at the surrounding context because I want to understand precisely what it is you meant by this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of my statement I stated that I had no contacts with any person from the DB and that there isn't anything I could say on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The investigator speaking to you in 2003, in relation to the DB was asking you about what role the DB had played in the events in the SBWS in 1991 and 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that your answer at paragraph 25 took into account both civilian and military matters concerning 1991 and 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I did not understand your question. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The -- when you answered that the DB had -- let me start that again. When you stated that you had no contact with the DB, who were you referring to when you said that "we had no contact with the DB?" Who was "we?"

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We of the government from the area. At least I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you say "the government," are you referring to -- just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you also referring to the national council which existed before the government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. As of the 7th of January when the national council was established in 1991 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you referring to issues concerning the JNA when you stated that you did not know what role the DB had played?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. The question was about the state security service, and I said what I said. I said that we had no contacts with them. As for the JNA, we did have contact with them, with the people who at that time were in the Sirmium-Baranja region.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you were saying that whatever the government or the national council was engaged in in the SBWS, it had, as far as you were aware, no contacts with the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And putting aside your direct contacts, the government's direct contacts with the DB, were you also saying that you did not know what role the DB had played and you had not been told what role they might have played; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you stand by that answer today?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you to other parts of your statement, P553, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some of your activities as paragraph 12 notes: "As the minister of the interior my first duty was to form the police station in the villages of Borovo Selo and Dalj. Our task was to find people and to choose those who would work there and also to provide them with uniforms, equipment, vehicles," et cetera. Are you with me, Mr. Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that your first duty was an urgent one because of the chaos which existed at that time in parts of the region of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand. I did not understand the question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It was important that you moved quickly to form a police station in both Borovo Selo and Dalj because civilians of all ethnicities were being harassed by, let me put it generally, men with guns; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so your task was an urgent one and your task required supplies which you didn't at that time possess; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were setting up police stations from scratch, if you understand that statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so you --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so you looked towards the Novi Sad SUP to provide some of those supplies to enable you to set up police stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the SUP provided some basic supplies to allow you to set up the police stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at paragraph 13 you state that part of those supplies included guns from the SUP Novi Sad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: From the warehouse I specified. That's where we received supplies from. It belonged to the SUP of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were those supplies used by police officers in the police stations that you refer to at paragraph 12 and 14?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did those police stations as a general rule bring some law and order to the SBWS region, or certainly those villages referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Not only in those villages, but in the villages surrounding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What specific role did you have once the police stations had been set up in relation to those police stations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted the people working for the police to do their work properly and fairly irrespective of the ethnic background of anyone, including those who had violated the law and who acted well beyond what one would consider normal in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you then in charge of these police stations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but they all had their own respective station commanders. At the ministry I also had a number of associates assisting me in doing everything properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On a day-to-day level were you making the operative operational decisions about how the police stations or how the commanders of the police station should work?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, together with my staff at the ministry we worked on that. I had people who had worked for the police for a number of years and who were familiar with many tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you attempting to protect only Serbians, or were you trying to protect civilians in general?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said a moment ago, it was our duty and obligation to protect all citizens living there, those who behaved properly, who did not do anything wrong and lived normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you personally in daily or weekly contact with Hadzic at this time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Perhaps not daily but at least weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: He never said that something was wrong. He seemed content with what I was doing, at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 14, Mr. Bogunovic, and the first statement there, the first sentence states: "After other areas were freed, there was a need for new stations to be set point up ..." Then there's a whole list of stations. What did you mean when you said "after other areas were freed?" Why did you use the word "freed?"

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I used the word "freed" because there were parts of that region which were inaccessible to us. There were barricades, and no movement was possible for civilians and Serbian civilians in particular to move about those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to pin-point with any accuracy when it was that the villages in the SBWS were freed, as you describe it? Was there a point in time when the government agreed that the villages had been freed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of September, we began liberating such locations, and Vukovar was freed sometime in November, around the 20th of November. That's the period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so by November or late November, early December, all the villages had been freed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as well as Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did the JNA leave the region?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA left the region, as far as I recall, towards the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And until they left the region, they were in effective command of the freeing of the villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you have a look at paragraph 23 of your statement P553, please. "We didn't notice the presence of the MUP of Serbia in the take-over of the villages. Everything was led by the army." Would you agree with me then what you saw and what you observed was the JNA and not the MUP of Serbia involved in freeing the villages?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the military and the Territorial Defence together were liberating the villages. The military administration ruled over the entire area up to the 23rd of December, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The remainder of the paragraph, paragraph 23 states: "Apart from Badza, Zavisic, and perhaps one or two other men, we didn't notice anyone else from MUP there." Would you agree with me that up until --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when Badza arrived, he -- no, let me strike that. When did Badza arrive in the SBWS region, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a long time ago. That was sometime around mid-August or perhaps even towards the end of August. Possibly even the beginning of September, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this around the time you were setting up the police stations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Badza come with members of a special unit from the public security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you find in the minutes to come a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where did he come from, as far as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, he had arrived from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Belgrade is a big place. What do you mean he came from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From what you observed when he arrived, did he assist with providing support to the setting up of the police stations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he did assist, and he told us what we should do to be safe, for all the civilians to be safe, or rather, for all the residents of the area to the safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So he moved around the police stations providing that expert advice?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He did move around the police stations that had been set up. He did have experience, and he was in a position to assist us. He was in a position to tell us what to do and how to best go about our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Putting aside -- and I'll come to this later, but putting aside his, from what you've described, somewhat overbearing attitude towards you and others, was he engaged in providing security to civilians in the SBWS region in the months after he arrived?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: By providing us with instructions and advice and so on and so forth, one could notice that he wanted to avoid problems in the liberated areas where the police stations had already been set up. He wanted things to be done in accordance with the law, in accordance to how he saw things should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that may be a convenient moment, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a convenient moment. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, at the very beginning of today's session, I referred to some documents which were already admitted into evidence but were nevertheless like to receive a chart. I do understand that on the transcript it's not audible, at least it doesn't appear that I also mentioned P384 and not only the other ones, therefore it's now on the record. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Bogunovic. Can I ask you to look again at your 2003 statement, P553, at paragraph 13. Sorry, paragraph 14. And the section I'm interested in is where it says: "All the equipment that was received came from Novi Sad. This included vehicles such as police Puch, four Land Rovers, and several luxury cars." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that the cars or the vehicles which came from Novi Sad had Serbian licence plates?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the vehicles did not have any registration plates at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The vehicles that came from Serbia, none of them had licence plates; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that those vehicles had registration plates. It was only later that we were provided with a registration plates for those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who provided the registration plates?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the plates that arrived from Novi Sad had M on them indicating they were coming from Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And those licence plates were given to all the vehicles that came from Serbia from the Novi Sad SUP?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And those vehicles were given to prominent persons involved this the security of the SBWS; is that correct? Such as police station commanders?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Ilija Kojic had one of those; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not from that contingent, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, what was different about his plate which also, as you told us, had an M on it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he did not get a vehicle from that contingent. He did get M registered plates, a vehicle, but I don't know whether it arrived from Novi Sad or from Belgrade, and I don't know who from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the plate he had was the same as the other plate, but just from a different contingent as you put it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The car that he got with registration plates, I don't know who he got it from, but that didn't go through the MUP, or at least, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the registration plate he had was the same as the registration plates relating to the cars from the Novi Sad SUP or different?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was an M registration plate. I don't know what the numbers were, but the M was exactly the same as on the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And when you said just a moment ago that "it didn't go through the MUP, or at least I didn't know about that," is it correct -- is there any reason why you wouldn't have known about that? Let me put it differently. Did you know about all the vehicles coming from the SUP from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I signed a receipt for those things that were handed over to me and I am aware of those vehicles. I don't know of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you were aware of the vehicles which came directly to the Ministry of the Interior? That was your remit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying is that I was in charge of those things that I took over. Ilija Kojic's vehicle was not one of those, therefore, I don't know where it had come from, how it had come to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, that we have P554 on the screen. And this is your statement of the 8th of February, 2007. And I want to look at paragraph 25, please, in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your statement says: "The first weapons that were brought and distributed to the Serbian villagers in the SAO SBWS area could not be brought there without the knowledge of the Serbian police. I do not have any direct information of the involvement of the MUP and the DB in this operation." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't hear your question. Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That wasn't a question yet. I was just checking whether you had read the relevant paragraph. Have you read paragraph 25?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How were these weapon -- let me strike that. When you describe the first weapons being brought into the Serbian villages, which period of time are you referring to approximately?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to a period after the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 2nd of May, and when you refer to the early, or sorry, the first weapons being brought, are you talking about throughout May on to June or I'm trying to establish what it is you mean about these first weapons and which period exactly, or approximately?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 1st of May, all we had were hunting rifles and some people had their own personal weapons. However, after the 2nd of May and after the incident in Borovo Selo we received a certain quantity of weapons from Serbia which arrived in the SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who received the weapons? When you say "we," who is we?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were Crisis Staffs in the villages which received whatever arrived, be it weapons, food, or something else. In other words, there were Crisis Staffs and their commanders, and the commanders and their men received all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were different Crisis Staffs making their own arrangements to receive these weapons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat. The reception is bad so I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm probably speaking too quietly. Did the different Crisis Staffs make their own arrangements to receive weapons in the period that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that things like that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, was there a co-ordination amongst the Crisis Staff to receive weapons, or were there different Crisis Staffs using their own staffs to make arrangements?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were co-ordinated efforts and things were brought to the villages that were threatened and that believed that they had to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you involved in the co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the Negoslavci Crisis Staff myself, and I was one of those who received some of the weapons at one point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did you receive the weapons from? How did you make the arrangement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you where the weapons came from. I didn't know any of those who had brought the weapons personally. In any case, the weapons were taken over in Sid. All the presidents of the Crisis Staffs were there and then they managed to transport the weapons that they had been issued with in any way they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, take your mind back to the time when the decision must have been made in your Crisis Staff to obtain weapons from Serbia. Who made the initial arrangements, or any of the arrangements?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The initial arrangements were made by the national council, or rather, its members. Goran and somebody else were earmarked and appointed to obtain weapons and protect people who were threatened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you must have spoken to Goran Hadzic about that, about those arrangements; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you must have been aware of the weapons arriving and being delivered to your Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you were vice-president of the national council; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what you've said, the national council was the -- excuse me if I'm para-phrasing, but the supervising body arranging the transfer of these weapons from Serbia to the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this occurred in May. Did it also occur in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May of 1991. Did it also occur in June?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did it occur after June?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later we also received a certain quantity of weapons by the military -- from the military rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a minute. I want to stick with these, how shall I put it, private arrangements with the Crisis Staff before the military get involved. Did that occur after June, the private arrangements with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know on how many occasions, but I believe that on three or four different occasions the weapons arrived throughout June, July, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the weapons -- sorry, let me start that again. Is this right: The military become involved after July and is that a response -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was it your observation that the weapons that had been supplied prior to the military becoming involved were old weapons or up-to-date weapons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The first batches involved old weapons, some of which was obsolete and no longer used by the police or the military. Those were Thompson and the so-called Spagins. It was only after the military started arriving that some other and better weapons arrived with them, like automatic and semi-automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you observed at the time that the weapons you were receiving through these private, what I've called private arrangements, were no longer used by the police in the SUP of Novi Sad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And are you able to give us an indication of how significant or insignificant the arrival of these old weapons were in terms of arming the population of the Serbian villages in the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was important because people felt a degree of safety and security. However, none of us knew at the time that those weapons were not in a good state of repairs, obsolete. Had we known at the time what we had received, I'm sure that the feeling would have been different, but at the time we felt safer because we had received weapons, although we didn't know what those weapons were, what they were like. I believe that actually nobody ever used those weapons ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And throughout your time as the vice-president of the national council and through the time of May, June, and July, you did not hear that this had anything to do with the Serbian MUP or the Serbian DB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I really can't say that that had anything to do either with the MUP or anybody else. I really don't know where the weapons came from. The weapons were rather old, obsolete, I don't know where it originated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go back to P553, please. The witness's first statement. And paragraph 72.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do we have paragraph 72. Page number is easier I am told. Page 12 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If would you have a look at 72, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Later when the JNA came they started distributing weapons. Through the TO they made lists of people, and assigned weapons to them." Could you elaborate on that, please, how this process took place and who it involved?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the JNA arrived, they immediately assumed command of the village. They provided weapons to the people who they believed were ready and willing to carry arms, who were willing to place themselves under their command and carry out tasks requested of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this was a part of the process of freeing the villages, as you described; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And securing them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was this process controlled by or supervised by the government or the national council?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: None of us could supervise that. Whatever we asked or required, there was the military command in place and we couldn't put any questions or conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "we couldn't put any questions," are you referring to the whole national council hierarchy up to Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know who in the JNA was making the decisions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain who made decisions. I know that the commander at the time was Mrksic, Sljivancanin was with him, and I heard of some other people, although I did not have occasion to speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to paragraph 56 of this statement, please. Or page 10 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I can just read quickly: "There were Territorial Defence staffs in the territories that were freed and they were responsible to the minister of defence Ilija Kojic. He was the one who co-ordinated the Territorial Defence with the JNA. He was responsible to the government, and he reported to the government. Ilija Kojic could not do anything without the knowledge of the JNA. Nothing could be done without the JNA's approval. He also had no influence over day-to-day operations and had no authority to give instructions to the TO on the ground." What role did Ilija Kojic play given that limitation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Kojic's role was to co-ordinate with TO staffs on behalf of his ministry to the extent possible at the moment. As I said already, nothing could be done without the army, without their decision or orders. Hence, during that period, he always had to wait for army decisions before conveying them further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Kojic have anything to do with distributing the weapons that were coming from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said that as if you were very certain. How are you so certain? I am not suggesting you are wrong, I'm just asking how you are certain.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: When the army brought in weapons, they had their own people distributing it. No one from the national council could be present or decide who the weapons were to be given to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if you are able to answer this, but by the time the JNA left, were the Serbian villages comprehensively armed, as you observed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA left there were many weapons in the Serbian villages and they were well armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 45, and we can go to it but we may not need to, of this statement, you refer to Kojic having been interfered with by Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let us go to it so you can see. Page 8 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's also deal with the first part of that paragraph since we are here. It's with reference to a meeting following the taking over of Vukovar, and if you need to go back in the statement to get context, please say so. This meeting was attended by Vojin Susa, Slavko Dokmanovic, Miodrag Crnogorac..." and so on. And then you note: "Although Arkan was not a member of government, he would occasionally attend meetings. It was my impression that he did that in order to control some of the ministers." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that you never saw Arkan, in fact, issue any orders to the government in meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that he did not issue orders. He provided suggestions on occasion, but at government sessions, he never issued orders. Only when there was a meeting in Vukovar, he insisted on some things that had to do with the prisoners, although I cannot recall that precisely. That was the only time his opinion conflicted however slightly that of those representing the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apart from Hadzic, was Arkan close to any other ministers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was close with any others. I think he was only close with Goran. He wasn't so close with the rest of us from the government. We did occasionally meet and greet, but there were no extensive contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In meetings did he appear -- let me start that again. In meetings did ministers other than Hadzic appear to appreciate his presence or tolerated it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell whether they appreciated it or not. We did tolerate him, and if he said something, none of us put up much resistance ever. We knew he wouldn't take that. So in a way we co-operated with him a little, although we did not want any extensive contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct though that your decisions as the minister of interior were not dictated to by Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, my decisions were not dictated by Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And going back to paragraph 45: "He was located," he as in Arkan, "was located 50 metres from the government building and interfered a lot, primarily with Ilija Kojic, minister of defence." What form did that interference take?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Arkan decided where to go by himself, he had some 2- to 300 of his men. And frequently he undertook his own activities, the reasons for which were only known to him. Such orders did not come from the army or anyone else. I think he did have discussions with Kojic, but he didn't pay much heed to what Kojic did. I think it was quite the other way. I think Kojic took what Arkan said much more than Arkan did in case of Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you use the word "interfere?"

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to indicate that he was meddling. I tried to picture a relationship between two people whereby one would try to talk the other into doing something and the other one can oppose or accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you give any concrete examples?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there was a plan for certain villages which at that time were still occupied to have them freed in one way, whereas Arkan would say that he didn't find that the best way possible and he wanted to do it the way he saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the JNA would be in charge of the taking over the villages. Kojic would answer to them and take suggestions from Arkan. Is that a fair summary of what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. The JNA did free the villages, they did. But Arkan did the same in some other villages with his men. The army did not take part in that, but I say this as -- well, it wasn't always the way Kojic had envisaged it, but Kojic certainly he could not resist Arkan in trying to stop him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Couldn't Kojic call on any armed men of his own to prevent Arkan from approaching it in the way he wanted?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We did not have the power to stop Arkan. Even certain JNA officers dared not stand up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many men did the JNA have, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say how many men they had. Many. But I think that they believed if they opposed Arkan, there would be a lot of people hurt and they rather let him do things his own way than have casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is this correct: Arkan and his 2- to 300 men promised a bloody battle if anyone stopped him and so the JNA and Kojic and the like chose not to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No direct threats were issued, but he frequently said that was under no obligation to listen to anyone and that he would do things the way he thought them best.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence of your answer, Mr. Bogunovic, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I said that he would not have anyone issue orders to him and that it could mean that there could be a clash resulting in casualties with people being hurt or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Isn't it also the case that Arkan was co-operating with senior members of Novi Sad corps? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was the extent of his co-operation with any organs of the Novi Sad corps. I only know that people from the TO as well as most of those from the army complained that he refused to co-operate and that he refused to undertake co-ordinated activities with the army. They said he always did things his own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you about -- just give me a moment. You know somebody or you knew somebody at the time called Radovan Kostic or Rade Kostic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the time, I didn't know Rade Kostic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did you come to know Rade Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you came to know him what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We met in the MUP building of the Sirmium-Baranja region.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So throughout 1991 and 1992, you had no dealings with Rade Kostic; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He never attended any government meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. At least he didn't introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He didn't give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see him giving anyone in the government any orders, 1992 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that person at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's absolutely ridiculous the idea that Kostic was above everybody in the SBWS government from your experience?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. I really don't remember him, and I never saw this man there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And your experience of him in 1993 was of somebody who might have been collecting information for the Serbian DB at some point in the past?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is possible, but I truly don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I notice the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is 7.00. Mr. Bogunovic, we will adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, but I would first like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow the 29th of June -- Tuesday the 29th of June, 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. We stand adjourned.
